questions.q: Define 'institutional interrelationship' in sociology and give one example from the NCERT text showing how a change in the economic sphere affected the family sphere.
questions.a: Institutional interrelationship means social institutions are mutually constitutive — change in one triggers adjustments in others. NCERT example: Post-1990 German unification withdrew family welfare schemes → economic insecurity rose → marriage rates declined sharply. A wrong answer treating institutions as isolated (e.g., "economy affects family but family doesn't affect economy") reveals a unidirectional, deterministic misunderstanding rather than reciprocal linkage.

questions.q: Explain why the functionalist view sees the nuclear family as 'best equipped' for industrial society, and why the NCERT text critiques this using Indian evidence.
questions.a: Functionalists (Parsons) argue nuclear family allows role specialisation: husband = instrumental/breadwinner, wife = affective/homemaker — fitting factory discipline and geographic mobility. NCERT critiques: (1) Indian nuclear families existed long before industrialisation among deprived castes; (2) A.M. Shah shows joint families *increased* post-Independence due to rising life expectancy; (3) Garment industry employs women as primary workers, contradicting 'male breadwinner' model. A wrong answer missing the empirical counter-evidence shows rote memorisation of Parsons without sociological evaluation.

questions.q: A tribal community in Odisha practices shifting cultivation. The state declares their forest a protected reserve, banning cultivation. Trace the effects through kinship, marriage, and religion in 4 steps.
questions.a: Step 1: Economic base destroyed → men migrate for wage labour → women become de facto household heads (female-headed households). Step 2: Kinship obligations shift — remittances replace collective labour; bride-price negotiations change as cash replaces land. Step 3: Marriage rules adapt — village exogamy weakens as migrants marry in urban settlements; age at marriage rises. Step 4: Forest deities lose ritual centrality; new workplace gods (e.g., factory safety rituals) emerge. A wrong answer listing only economic effects shows failure to see institutional feedback loops.

questions.q: Compare how Weber's Protestant Ethic thesis and the Nasik pilgrimage example (NCERT) differently conceptualise the religion-economy link. Which better explains contemporary Indian temple economies?
questions.a: Weber: Religion (Calvinist predestination anxiety) → psychological driver → capitalist investment/rational profit-seeking (ideational causation). Nasik: Pilgrimage demand → creates craft occupations (coppersmiths) → market fluctuations push artisans into wage labour → religious specialists' children enter secular education (material causation). For contemporary Indian temple economies (Tirupati, Vaishno Devi), Nasik's model fits better: religious rituals generate massive service-sector employment, real estate, and political patronage networks — economic interests shape temple administration, not just theology. A wrong answer treating them as identical misses the directionality of causation.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Education in modern India reproduces caste and gender inequality rather than promoting meritocracy." Use functionalist and conflict perspectives with NCERT evidence.
questions.a: Functionalist (Durkheim): Education transmits universalistic values, selects talent for roles — meritocratic ideal. Conflict (Pathak, Pratichi report): Privileged schools teach confidence; SC/ST girls drop out during cultivation season for dung collection/domestic work; schooling *intensifies* elite-mass divide. Evaluation: Conflict perspective better explains Indian reality — 10-year-old Dalit girl picking cow dung cannot access the 'common base' Durkheim assumes. A wrong answer giving only one perspective or ignoring the Pratichi evidence shows inability to weigh theoretical frameworks against empirical data.

questions.q: Design a mini-research question to study how the 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) affected marriage strategies among Muslim families in Assam. Specify: (a) which three institutions you would examine, (b) one hypothesis linking them, (c) one method.
questions.a: (a) Polity (citizenship law), Family/Marriage (spouse selection), Kinship (cross-border networks). (b) Hypothesis: CAA-induced citizenship anxiety accelerates endogamous marriage within documented lineages and discourages cross-border (Bangladesh) affinal ties to avoid statelessness risk for offspring. (c) Method: Semi-structured interviews with 20 Muslim women in Barak Valley + analysis of Nikahnama records pre/post-2019. Good answer shows operationalising institutional interrelationship into testable design. Poor answer picks unrelated institutions or proposes untestable hypothesis.

Fill in the blank: Imagine a young woman from a rural village in Maharashtra who migrates to ______ to work in a garment export factory.

questions.a: The student must be able to trace a specific macro-level change (e.g., industrialisation, migration, legal reform) through at least three interconnected institutions, explaining the causal mechanism at each step using sociological concepts (e.g., division of labour, patriarchy, secularisation, citizenship rights), and evaluate whether.
